Learning notes · GPU kernels · Study 1 · Nov 2026
Question: two kernels on two CUDA streams share one GPU. When does the second one get SMs?
Hardware: one NVIDIA B200, 148 SMs, compute capability 10.0 (sm_100)
Tools: CUDA C++ (nvcc), PyTorch streams and profiler, %globaltimer/%smid per-block stamps, Perfetto; a Triton companion run
Status: study notes. Each configuration has one profiled run (the timelines below) plus 20 unprofiled repeats per launch order (the medians). Observed behavior on this device, not a guarantee about every CUDA device.
TL;DR
A stream is an ordering promise, not a reservation. Work in one stream runs in order; two streams promise nothing about each other, and neither owns any SMs. A thread block lands on an SM only when the whole block fits (threads, registers, shared memory, block slots). Once there, it stays on that SM until it exits. A cooperative grid was admitted all at once. With 144 cooperative blocks waiting and only 52 free SMs, nothing started. The grid started (all 144 blocks within 0.6 µs) as soon as 144 SMs were free: at 3.1 ms with four long-running B blocks, at 4.6 ms with five. An ordinary launch of the same grid started in about 17 µs on the 52 free SMs and ran in waves. The 1 ms “grid sync” slices were waiting, not barrier cost. One block arrived 1 ms late; the release took about 0.13 µs across all 144 SMs. A grid barrier keeps finished blocks on their SMs. With A launched first, the barrier made B’s regular blocks finish about 1 ms later. Part 1: from launch to an SM Before the experiment, here is the path a kernel launch takes, from the top. The CUDA programming model is documented, and so are the occupancy limits. The hardware scheduler below the driver largely isn’t, so when I describe it I say where the description comes from.
What a stream actually promises A CUDA stream is a queue of work with one rule: operations in the same stream run in the order they were issued, and each finishes before the next starts. Operations in different streams have no ordering between them unless you add one (events, cudaStreamWaitEvent, a synchronize). That is the whole contract. A stream doesn’t own SMs, doesn’t reserve memory bandwidth and has no priority unless you create it with one.
In PyTorch the same idea looks like this. It is the shape of the harness used below:
s_a, s_b = torch.cuda.Stream(), torch.cuda.Stream() with torch.cuda.stream(s_b): launch_b() # returns as soon as the launch is queued with torch.cuda.stream(s_a): launch_a() # also returns immediately; no wait between the two torch.cuda.synchronize() # the host blocks here, once, until both are done Kernel launches are asynchronous. The host call returns when the launch is queued, not when the kernel starts. In the profiled runs below, cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel returned in about 6 µs, even in the run where the GPU didn’t start that kernel for another 3.1 ms. The host-side trace shows none of the waiting.
What the driver does with a launch Below cudaLaunchKernel there are a few layers. This is how NVIDIA’s open-source kernel driver and its published hardware headers describe them. The exact details vary by GPU generation.
flowchart TB A["<b>CPU</b> · your code, CUDA runtime<br/>cudaLaunchKernel"] --> D["<b>CPU</b> · CUDA driver<br/>cuLaunchKernel"] D -- "write launch commands" --> PB[("<b>memory</b> · pushbuffer")] D -- "append pointer, ring doorbell" --> GF["<b>memory</b> · GPFIFO of one channel"] PB -.-> H GF -- "GPU fetches" --> H["<b>GPU</b> · host interface<br/>fetch + decode commands"] H --> FE["<b>GPU</b> · compute front end<br/>pending grids from all channels"] FE --> WD["<b>GPU</b> · work distributor"] WD -- "one block at a time, when it fits" --> SM[("<b>GPU</b> · SMs")] The launch path, as publicly described. The host only writes commands into memory and tells the GPU where to find them. Everything after the doorbell happens on the GPU, without the CPU. Channel. A channel is the GPU’s unit of command submission: an independent command queue belonging to one context. The driver creates channels for a context and maps streams onto them. Pushbuffer. A launch becomes a short sequence of commands (“methods”) written into a buffer in memory. For a compute launch, the core of it is a descriptor of the grid: grid and block dimensions, shared memory size, register count, kernel entry point and parameters. NVIDIA’s open headers call this descriptor a QMD. GPFIFO and doorbell. The driver appends a pointer to the new pushbuffer segment to the channel’s GPFIFO, a ring buffer of such pointers. It then writes a doorbell register to tell the GPU there’s new work. On current GPUs this happens from user space, with no system call per launch. Host interface. The GPU fetches GPFIFO entries, reads the pushbuffer, decodes the methods and forwards compute work to the compute engine’s front end. Streams, connections and Hyper-Q How many independent queues does the GPU see? Since Kepler, NVIDIA GPUs have had several hardware-managed queues (“Hyper-Q”; the GK110 whitepaper says 32). The CUDA driver multiplexes your streams onto a pool of them. The size of that pool is documented as an environment variable: CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS (default 8, up to 32). If you have more busy streams than connections, two unrelated streams can end up in one hardware queue and serialize behind each other even though the API says they’re independent. This experiment uses only two streams, so it never comes close.
Admission: when does a block get an SM? The GPU doesn’t schedule a kernel onto SMs. It schedules thread blocks (CTAs). The Kepler whitepaper names a Grid Management Unit and a CUDA Work Distributor for this job. Current generations don’t publish an equivalent block diagram, so I’ll call it “the work distributor” and describe only what’s documented or measured:
Pending grids, possibly from several streams, wait in the front end. The distributor takes the next block of a runnable grid and looks for an SM where the whole block fits in what is still free. The block is placed. It stays on that SM, holding its resources, until every thread in it exits. Blocks don’t migrate and don’t get partially admitted. (Compute preemption, which saves and restores a whole context when the GPU time-slices between processes, is the exception; it doesn’t come up here.) When a block exits, its resources free up and the next block (from any eligible grid) can use them. “Fits” means every per-SM limit at once. These are the limits for this B200. The first four come straight from the device properties in the profiler trace:
Per-SM resource (cc 10.0) Limit Used per block in this study Threads 2,048 32 (one warp) Registers 65,536 16 / thread → 512 Shared memory 233,472 B (228 KiB) B: 232,448 B · A: 229,316 B Max shared memory one block may opt into 232,448 B (227 KiB) (B asks for exactly this) Resident blocks 32 1 So the shared-memory request is what decides admission. The CUDA programming guide also says the system reserves 1 KiB of shared memory per resident block on recent GPUs. With that included, a B block needs 232,448 + 1,024 = 233,472 B, exactly one whole SM. An A block needs 230,340 B, so two of anything don’t fit on one SM. Each SM can hold one block from either kernel, never two. The 148 SMs become 148 slots, which makes the arithmetic of the experiment visible.
That’s a deliberate setup, not the normal case. A small block with no shared-memory request uses a sliver of each limit, so many blocks, from different kernels, can share one SM. The Triton companion run at the end shows exactly that.
Admission order (which block goes to which SM, and which of two runnable grids wins a free SM) is not specified by CUDA. The SM numbers in the timelines below are just what happened here.
Cooperative launches cooperative_groups::this_grid().sync() is a barrier across every block of a grid. It can only work if all blocks are resident at the same time: a block that has not been admitted can’t arrive, and blocks spinning at the barrier would never exit to make room for it. CUDA therefore requires grid-wide sync to be launched with cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel. That call rejects grids larger than what the device can hold at once (cudaErrorCooperativeLaunchTooLarge), computed from the occupancy calculator. Here that’s 1 block/SM × 148 SMs = 148 ≥ 144, so the launch is legal.
The documentation guarantees co-residency, but it doesn’t say how the guarantee is met when another stream is already occupying SMs. A legal 144-block cooperative grid could arrive while only 52 SMs are free. That’s the question the experiment asks.
Part 2: the experiment Setup Two kernels, two streams, one GPU, and nothing else on it (checked with nvidia-smi first):
B: 96 ordinary blocks on its own stream. Every B block spins for 3 ms, then a 0.1 ms tail. Blocks 0–3 are stragglers: they spin 3 ms longer (6 ms total). In the five-straggler variant, block 4 spins 1.5 ms longer (4.5 ms). A: 144 blocks on another stream, launched cooperatively in the main arms. Every A block spins for 2 ms; block 0 spins 3 ms (a deliberate late arrival). Then comes an optional this_grid().sync(), then a 0.1 ms tail, except block 1, whose tail is 0.6 ms. One block per SM for both kernels, forced by the shared-memory sizes above. Submission order: B then A (“B first”) or A then B, with no wait between the two launches. Three configurations of A, each run with four and five stragglers and in both launch orders:
Arm A launch Grid barrier in A coop1-sync1 cooperative yes coop1-sync0 cooperative no coop0-sync0 ordinary cudaLaunchKernel no (an ordinary launch can’t use one) The cooperative-without-barrier arm separates the two choices. It shows whether the launch mode alone changes admission, or whether the barrier does.
What should happen Count SMs with B submitted first. At t ≈ 0, B’s 96 blocks take 96 SMs and 52 are free. A needs 144.
Hypothesis 1: all-or-nothing admission. To keep its co-residency promise, a cooperative grid starts only when all of its blocks can be placed. The regular B blocks end at 3 ms + 0.1 ms ≈ 3.1 ms. That leaves 4 stragglers, so 148 − 4 = 144 free, exactly enough. Prediction: A starts at ≈ 3.1 ms, every block at nearly the same moment, on every SM except the four straggler SMs. With five stragglers, 148 − 5 = 143 < 144, so A must wait for the fifth one to end at 4.5 + 0.1 ≈ 4.6 ms. Hypothesis 2: incremental admission. Cooperative blocks are placed as SMs free up, like ordinary ones. Prediction: A starts within tens of µs on the 52 free SMs, the rest trickle in, and the barrier simply waits longer. In this particular setup that wouldn’t even deadlock, because B eventually finishes. In general it could, which is why I expected Hypothesis 1. Control: ordinary A. No co-residency promise, so A should start almost immediately on the 52 free SMs and run in waves: 52 blocks, then more as A’s own 2 ms blocks finish, then the rest when B’s regular blocks free 92 SMs at 3.1 ms. 0 148 SMs t ≈ 0 B just started B: 96 blocks (one per SM) 52 free A needs 144 SMs at once → 52 < 144. Cooperative A cannot start; an ordinary A could start on the 52. t ≈ 3.1 ms 4 stragglers left 144 free → A admitted (all 144 blocks within 0.6 µs) 148 − 4 = 144 ≥ 144. The grid fits exactly; the four straggler SMs are the only ones A avoids. t ≈ 3.1 ms 5 stragglers left 143 free → still waiting 148 − 5 = 143 < 144. A waits for the fifth straggler, which ends at ≈ 4.6 ms; A starts then. busy with a B block free, but not enough for A free, and enough for all of A The SM budget under Hypothesis 1. Because each SM holds exactly one block, the question “does A fit?” becomes “are 144 of the 148 SMs free?”. Four stragglers leave exactly 144 free; five leave 143. The kernel and how it’s instrumented The whole kernel is a timed spin with an optional barrier. What matters is where it records time. One compiled kernel serves as both A and B: the delay argument tells it which one it is. The captured source packs every per-block duration into a single nested ternary. Below, those durations are pulled out into two small helpers with the same values, and comments are added; the rest is the captured source, lightly reformatted:
#include <cooperative_groups.h> constexpr unsigned long long US = 1000, MS = 1000 * US; // %globaltimer counts nanoseconds __device__ unsigned long long timer() { // GPU-wide nanosecond clock unsigned long long v; asm volatile("mov.u64 %0, %%globaltimer;" : "=l"(v)); return v; } // How long a block spins before the (optional) barrier. // B is launched with delay = -4 or -5 (that many stragglers); A with delay = 2 ms. __device__ unsigned long long work_ns(int block, int delay) { bool is_b = delay < 0; if (is_b) { int stragglers = -delay; if (block < 4) return 6 * MS; // stragglers 0-3 if (stragglers == 5 && block == 4) return 4 * MS + 500 * US; // 5th straggler return 3 * MS; // regular B block } if (block == 0) return delay + 1 * MS; // A block 0 reaches the barrier 1 ms late return delay; // every other A block: 2 ms } // How long a block spins after the barrier. __device__ unsigned long long tail_ns(int block, int delay) { bool is_a = delay >= 0; if (is_a && block == 1) return 600 * US; // A block 1: long tail return 100 * US; // everyone else } extern "C" __global__ void toy(unsigned long long *out, int barrier, int delay) { int block = blockIdx.x; unsigned sm; asm volatile("mov.u32 %0, %%smid;" : "=r"(sm)); // which SM this block landed on auto start = timer(); while (timer() - start < work_ns(block, delay)) {} // "work" auto arrival = timer(); if (barrier) cooperative_groups::this_grid().sync(); // A only auto passed = timer(); while (timer() - passed < tail_ns(block, delay)) {} // "tail" if (threadIdx.x == 0) { // one row per block: [sm, t0, t1, t2, t3] out += 5 * block; out[0] = sm; out[1] = start; out[2] = arrival; out[3] = passed; out[4] = timer(); } } The launcher picks ordinary or cooperative launch and passes the stream handle from PyTorch:
extern "C" int launch(void *out, int count, int barrier, int coop, int delay, int smem, void *stream) { void *args[] = {&out, &barrier, &delay}; // allow up to 227 KiB of dynamic shared memory per block cudaFuncSetAttribute(toy, cudaFuncAttributeMaxDynamicSharedMemorySize, 232448); if (coop) return cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel((void *)toy, dim3(count), dim3(32), args, smem, (cudaStream_t)stream); return cudaLaunchKernel((void *)toy, dim3(count), dim3(32), args, smem, (cudaStream_t)stream); } It’s compiled with nvcc -arch=sm_100 -rdc=true -shared (grid sync needs relocatable device code) and loaded with ctypes. A runs with 229,316 B of dynamic shared memory per block and B with 232,448 B. The Python side does a warm-up of each launch, then one profiled iteration:
with torch.profiler.profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof: for i in ((1, 0) if b_first else (0, 1)): # submit both, no wait in between launch(i) # each on its own torch.cuda.Stream torch.cuda.synchronize() prof.export_chrome_trace(name + ".json") # kernel-level view (one slice per kernel) torch.save([t.cpu() for t in out], name + ".pt") # block-level stamps, same iteration Then 20 unprofiled trials per launch order, alternating the order between trials to reduce order bias. The trials record summary numbers such as “first A start − first B start” and “B blocks still running when A started”.
What the stamps do and don’t mean. %globaltimer is a GPU-wide clock (it advanced in 32 ns steps here), so stamps from different SMs are comparable. A block’s start is when its first instruction ran, not when the hardware decided to admit it. Likewise end is a stamp just before exit. Each “block” bar below is therefore an instrumented interval, slightly inside the true residency. Only thread 0 writes, so each block produces exactly one row.
From stamps to a timeline. A short script turns each [blocks, 5] tensor into a Chrome trace that Perfetto can open: one lane per block with three slices (work, sync or gap, tail), plus a live-block counter (+1 at each start, −1 at each end). Times are relative to the earliest block start:
for block, (sm, start, arrival, passed, end) in enumerate(rows): lane = dict(pid=kernel_id, tid=block + 1) for phase, l, r in [("work", start, arrival), ("grid sync" if barrier else "no barrier", arrival, passed), ("tail", passed, end)]: events.append(dict(**lane, ph="X", name=phase, ts=(l - origin) / 1000, dur=(r - l) / 1000, args={"SM": sm, "block": block})) The viewers below draw the same data in the page. Each one has Open in Perfetto, which builds this trace in your browser and hands it to ui.perfetto.dev (via Perfetto’s documented postMessage API), and Embed Perfetto, which loads the Perfetto UI inline.
How to read the viewers: Rows: SMs draws one row per SM, so you can see which kernel held each SM and when. Rows: blocks draws one row per block (A first, then B). Hover for the stamps, drag across the plot to zoom in time. The two lines at the top count live blocks of A (blue) and B (orange). The run menu switches between all twelve configurations. The Perfetto buttons load ui.perfetto.dev, a separate app hosted by Google. The trace is built in your browser and passed to it directly; this page doesn’t upload it anywhere.
Walking through the traces The kernel-level view hides the reason The PyTorch trace has one slice per kernel. For the four-straggler, barrier, B-first run (times relative to the first runtime call; the first cudaFuncSetAttribute took about 1.6 ms, a one-time cost):
Event Starts at Duration cudaLaunchKernel (B) 1,599.3 µs 19.0 µs cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel (A) 1,662.3 µs 6.2 µs B kernel on GPU (96 blocks, stream 17) 1,618.3 µs 6,101.7 µs A kernel on GPU (144 blocks, stream 13) 4,719.3 µs 3,602.3 µs A was submitted 44 µs after B started, and the host call returned in 6 µs. The A kernel slice starts 3.1 ms later. From this view alone you could guess “the streams serialized” or “the driver delayed the launch”. The block-level view shows what actually held it up.
Four stragglers: A waits for exactly 144 free SMs Interactive timeline needs JavaScript. Four stragglers, cooperative A with grid sync, B submitted first. In SM view, orange B bars fill SMs 0–89 and 142–147; SMs 90–141 sit empty for 3.1 ms although A is waiting. A (blue) starts on 144 SMs at once. The only SMs it never uses are 142–145, where the four stragglers are still running. In this profiled run:
B’s 96 blocks landed on SMs 0–89 and 142–147. SMs 90–141 (52 of them) were idle for 3.1 ms while a 144-block grid was waiting. The 92 regular B blocks ended at ≈ 3.10 ms. The first A block started at 3,101.0 µs, and all 144 had started within 0.6 µs of each other. At that moment exactly 4 B blocks were still running, on SMs 142–145. A ran on all 148 SMs except those four. The 20 repeated trials agree. Every B-first median shows A starting 3.1 ms after B with 4 B blocks still live, with or without the grid barrier:
B submitted first (median of 20) First A start after first B start, 4 / 5 stragglers B blocks still live at first A start, 4 / 5 Cooperative A, grid sync 3.101 / 4.600 ms 4 / 4 Cooperative A, no grid sync 3.101 / 4.600 ms 4 / 4 Ordinary A 0.017 / 0.016 ms 96 / 96 Hypothesis 1 holds, and the barrier doesn’t matter for admission. The cooperative launch is what makes A wait. A cooperative grid that never calls grid.sync() is held back just the same.
Five stragglers: 143 free SMs is not enough Switch the viewer above to 5 stragglers · A cooperative + grid sync · B submitted first. Now 148 − 5 = 143, one SM short. A doesn’t start at 3.1 ms. It starts at 4,600.8 µs, right after the fifth straggler (4.5 ms of work + 0.1 ms tail) ends. When it starts, the other four stragglers are still running, so again exactly 4 B blocks are live. A then uses the fifth straggler’s SM (146) and avoids SMs 142–145. The medians: 4.600 ms with or without the barrier.
This is the cleanest evidence for all-or-nothing admission. The start time is set by the moment the free-SM count reaches 144, not by when “B is done” or “most of B is done”.
Control: an ordinary A starts immediately Interactive timeline needs JavaScript. Same grid, ordinary launch, B submitted first. A starts on the 52 free SMs 57 µs after B in this run (17 µs median), then refills those SMs as its own 2 ms blocks finish. The last wave lands on B’s SMs after 3.1 ms. With cudaLaunchKernel there’s no co-residency promise, so the distributor uses whatever is free. A started 57 µs after B in this run (median 17 µs over 20 trials) while all 96 B blocks were still running. It ran in three waves: 52 blocks at once, 51 more between ≈ 2.1 and 2.7 ms on those same SMs as A’s own blocks finished, and the last 41 at ≈ 3.1 ms on SMs that B had freed. The median trial started 103 A blocks before the first B block exited. That count is cumulative across waves, not simultaneous residency.
The ordinary A finished at ≈ 5.2 ms in this run. The cooperative A, which waited, finished at ≈ 6.2 ms (no barrier) or ≈ 6.7 ms (barrier). Gang admission has a cost when the GPU is shared.
Inside the barrier: arrival imbalance, not barrier cost Interactive timeline needs JavaScript. Block view of the cooperative grid. Drag across the region from 5 to 6.8 ms to zoom. Every A block spends ≈ 2 ms working, then hatched ≈ 1 ms at the grid sync. Block 0 works 3 ms and spends almost nothing at the sync. Block 1’s tail runs 0.6 ms instead of 0.1 ms. The long “grid sync” slices look like an expensive barrier. They aren’t:
Block 0 does 1 ms more work by design, so it arrives 1 ms late. Every other block arrives at ≈ 2 ms and waits about 1.0 ms (median max wait 1.0008 ms). Block 0 itself waits ≈ 1 µs. Once block 0 arrives, the release is fast. All 144 blocks left the barrier within 0.13 µs of each other in this run. After the barrier, block 1 spins 0.6 ms instead of 0.1 ms. There’s no second barrier, so nobody waits for it. It only stretches the kernel’s end by 0.5 ms (median exit spread 500 µs), and every other block exits on time. Before blaming a long sync slice on synchronization overhead, compare arrival times across blocks. The slice length mostly measures how late the slowest block arrived.
A first: the barrier holds SMs hostage Interactive timeline needs JavaScript. A submitted first. A takes 144 SMs immediately; B’s first four blocks (the stragglers) take the 4 spare SMs. The other 92 B blocks wait for A’s SMs. With the grid sync they wait until ≈ 3.1 ms; without it, until A’s blocks exit at ≈ 2.1 ms. Flip the order and A gets the GPU first in every configuration (ordinary or cooperative makes no difference when the SMs are empty). B gets only the 4 spare SMs, and its first four blocks, the stragglers, take them. The question is when the other 92 B blocks get in:
No grid sync: A blocks exit at ≈ 2.1 ms (block 0 at 3.1 ms), and B’s blocks move in right away. The last regular B block ended at ≈ 5.2 ms. Grid sync: every A block sits at the barrier until block 0 arrives at 3 ms, keeping its SM the whole time. The last regular B block ended at ≈ 6.2 ms. Those are single profiled runs. The B-last-end numbers are dominated by the 6.1 ms stragglers in both cases, so the repeated-trial spans hide the difference. In the timeline, the extra 1 ms of hatched “waiting” in A is 1 ms that 140-odd SMs could have spent on B.
Companion: Triton, many blocks per SM An earlier round of runs tried the same two-stream idea in Triton, before the straggler version existed. Same shape: A is 144 cooperative blocks that spin 2 ms (block 0 spins 3 ms), B is 96 ordinary blocks that spin 3 ms, and every block writes the same five stamps. The kernel, lightly reformatted, with comments added:
@triton.jit def stamp(): # %globaltimer, as in the CUDA version return tl.inline_asm_elementwise("mov.u64 $0, %globaltimer;", constraints="=l", args=[], dtype=tl.uint64, is_pure=False, pack=1) @triton.jit def toy(out, counter, count: tl.constexpr, barrier: tl.constexpr, delay: tl.constexpr): idx = tl.program_id(0) # Triton's name for blockIdx.x start = stamp() sm = tl.inline_asm_elementwise("mov.u32 $0, %smid;", constraints="=r", args=[], dtype=tl.uint32, is_pure=False, pack=1) while stamp() - start < delay + (idx == 0) * 1000000: # "work"; block 0 +1 ms pass arrival = stamp() if barrier: # hand-rolled grid barrier: tl.atomic_add(counter, 1, sem="acq_rel", scope="gpu") # "I'm here" while tl.atomic_add(counter, 0, sem="acquire", scope="gpu") < count: pass # wait for all passed = stamp() while stamp() - passed < 100000 + (idx == 1) * 500000: # "tail"; block 1 +0.5 ms pass tl.store(out + idx * 5, sm) # one row per block: [sm, t0, t1, t2, t3] tl.store(out + idx * 5 + 1, start) tl.store(out + idx * 5 + 2, arrival) tl.store(out + idx * 5 + 3, passed) tl.store(out + idx * 5 + 4, stamp()) Each kernel is launched on its own stream, with A as a cooperative grid:
toy[(count,)](out, counter, count, barrier, delay, num_warps=1, # 32 threads per block launch_cooperative_grid=is_a) # A: cooperative launch; B: ordinary Three differences from the CUDA version matter:
No shared-memory carveout. Nothing asks for 227 KiB per block, so a block is just one warp of 32 threads with whatever registers Triton chose. The barrier is an atomic counter, not this_grid().sync(). Each block bumps the counter, then spins until it reaches count. This is only safe because of the cooperative launch: if some A block were never admitted, everyone else would spin forever on SMs it needs. The counter is reset between runs. One kernel body for both A and B, so B’s block 0 and block 1 get the same tweaks as A’s, and B has no stragglers. Why several blocks now fit on one SM. Run the admission check from Part 1 on a Triton block: 32 threads out of 2,048, no shared memory to speak of, one of 32 block slots. Threads alone would allow 64 blocks per SM; the 32-slot limit caps it at 32, unless registers bind first (65,536 ÷ 32 threads ÷ 32 blocks = 64 registers per thread; Triton’s actual register count wasn’t recorded). Either way an SM that already holds a B block has plenty left for an A block. So the free capacity on the GPU at t ≈ 0 isn’t “52 SMs”; it’s room for well over 144 more blocks.
Interactive timeline needs JavaScript. Triton companion run (earlier round), B submitted first, no barrier. No large shared-memory request, so blocks from both kernels share SMs. A starts ≈ 0.12 ms after B, on SMs where B blocks are still running. In Rows: SMs, an SM that holds two blocks at once is drawn as two thin lanes, one per block. What the trace shows:
A started while all 96 B blocks were still running. All 144 A blocks started within 0.6 µs of each other, about 0.12 ms after the first B block. B’s first block exit came at 3.1 ms. The 0.12 ms gap is probably the host-side gap between two Triton launches; it wasn’t measured. 92 SMs held one A block and one B block at the same time. No SM ever held more than two. That’s the tightest possible packing: 144 + 96 = 240 blocks on 148 SMs means at least 240 − 148 = 92 SMs have to double up, and exactly 92 did. Here the distributor spread blocks across SMs instead of stacking them. That’s observed, not documented. This is consistent with gang admission, not a counterexample. The cooperative grid still started all at once. It just didn’t have to wait, because all 144 blocks fit on top of B immediately. The lesson: “free SM” means free resources, not “an SM with nothing on it”. The carveout in the main experiment is what turned SMs into whole slots and made the waiting visible. This isn’t a matched replication of the straggler experiment: there are no stragglers, and the barrier is different.
What I’m confident about, and what I’m not Claim Basis Launches are async; same-stream order only CUDA programming guide Blocks are admitted whole and stay on their SM until exit CUDA programming model; consistent with every block here (one SM ID per row) Per-SM limits and the 1 KiB reserved per block Device properties in the trace; CUDA programming guide Channels, pushbuffers, GPFIFO, doorbells, QMD NVIDIA’s open-source driver and published headers; details vary by generation A cooperative grid started only when all 144 blocks could be resident Measured here: 3.1 / 4.6 ms thresholds, 0.6 µs start spread, avoided exactly the straggler SMs Where that wait happens (driver vs. front end vs. distributor) Unknown. The stamps can’t see it. The host call returned in 6 µs, so the host wasn’t blocking. This behavior on other GPUs, drivers or with MPS / green contexts Not tested Lessons Streams give ordering, not capacity. Two “concurrent” streams share one pool of SMs, and whoever holds an SM keeps it until its block exits. Admission is about whole blocks fitting. Big shared-memory or register footprints turn SMs into coarse slots. That’s what made this experiment readable, and it’s what makes real kernels block each other. A cooperative launch is gang-scheduled in practice. It waits for room for the entire grid, even with no grid.sync() in the code, and even while many SMs sit idle. If you share a GPU with other streams, size cooperative grids below the SM count you can actually expect to be free. Kernel-level traces show when, block-level traces show why. The PyTorch trace showed A starting 3.1 ms late. Per-block %smid + %globaltimer stamps showed the four SMs it was waiting on. Read barrier slices as arrival skew first. A 1 ms sync slice here was one late block, not a slow barrier. Barriers hold resources. Blocks waiting at a grid barrier are resident and keep their SMs, which delays other streams’ work. Change one thing at a time, and repeat. Each claim above comes from comparing arms that differ in exactly one flag, with medians of 20 alternating-order trials, not a single trace. Open questions and next steps Where is the cooperative grid held? In the driver, the front end or the distributor? Nsight Systems’ GPU trace, or launching from a CUDA graph, might separate those. Unequal stragglers. A variant with three +3 ms stragglers and one +5 ms straggler is written but not run. The prediction: A still starts at ≈ 3.1 ms, because that’s when the free-SM count reaches 144, however long the four stragglers keep running after that. Priorities. Does a high-priority stream let an ordinary grid jump ahead of a waiting cooperative grid on newly freed SMs? Reproducing it On any idle GPU with 148 SMs and sm_100 (other SM counts need the block counts adjusted), check nvidia-smi first. Then run one arm per configuration:
DEMO=cuda OUT="$PWD/out" COOP=1 BARRIER=1 STRAGGLERS=4 python3 demo.py # coop + grid sync DEMO=cuda OUT="$PWD/out" COOP=1 BARRIER=0 STRAGGLERS=4 python3 demo.py # coop, no sync DEMO=cuda OUT="$PWD/out" COOP=0 BARRIER=0 STRAGGLERS=4 python3 demo.py # ordinary Each run writes the PyTorch trace, the per-block tensors for both launch orders, and the 20-trial summary.
Sources NVIDIA, CUDA C++ Programming Guide: streams and asynchronous execution, cooperative groups and grid synchronization, compute-capability limits and reserved shared memory. NVIDIA, CUDA Runtime API: cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel, cudaFuncSetAttribute. NVIDIA, CUDA environment variables: CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS. NVIDIA, Kepler GK110 architecture whitepaper (2012): Hyper-Q, Grid Management Unit, work distributor. NVIDIA, open-gpu-kernel-modules and open-gpu-doc: channels, GPFIFO, pushbuffer methods, QMD layouts. NVIDIA, PTX ISA: %globaltimer, %smid. Perfetto docs: opening traces from another page via postMessage.
summary: How a CUDA launch travels from a stream to an SM, what decides whether a thread block is admitted, and a two-stream experiment on a B200 showing that a cooperative grid starts only when all of its blocks fit at once.
title: How to Reason About CUDA Streams and Block Admission

SGLang fireside chat · Structured notes · Nov 2026
Speaker: Bill Jia, VP Eng, Core ML/AI, Google (previously Meta, where he led AI infra including PyTorch)
Notes: paraphrased, not verbatim
TL;DR
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is now a core part of how infrastructure gets built. Bill’s answer to “one free week of GCP” was to use agents to write kernels, then use the speedup to win back more compute. He said the same loop is speeding up chip design (layout, simulators, firmware, compilers) and model releases. Google decided to sell TPUs to the industry, not keep them in-house. After internal debate that reached Sundar Pichai and the board, Google aligned about 1.5 years ago on selling TPUs outside the company. Bill’s view is that the industry needs competition, and that matters more than Google’s revenue. The main gap now is the software ecosystem, not chip performance. The TPU’s strength is scale. 64-chip ICI cubes are joined by optical circuit switches into 9,216-chip (Ironwood) or 9,600-chip (TPU 8t) superpods. The Virgo network stretches this toward 1M chips, and all the network management is handled in software. Training and inference silicon have split. TPU 8t targets training. TPU 8i targets inference, with 3× more on-chip SRAM to hold the KV cache, a Boardfly topology, and a collectives engine that replaces SparseCore. TPU 8i Max puts two dies in one package. TPU 8tx adds AMD EPYC hosts for confidential computing. Bill thinks we are underbuilding. He placed AI at about where the internet was in 1997. Coding agents work, but he said the “at your fingertips” consumer products haven’t appeared yet. One free week of GCP Host: What would you do with one free week of GCP resources?
What Bill said
Use this one week to generate more resources.
With enough focus, performance can always be improved. He sees the ultimate way to write kernels as removing the middle abstraction layers and having agents write kernels directly, which is RSI, or ML improving ML. This takes a lot more compute up front. The kernel speedups then free up chips that can go to other work. Context
The TPU’s kernel language is Pallas, a JAX extension that targets both TPU and GPU. SGLang’s TPU backends run on Pallas kernels written by RadixArk, Google, and the community. This is the layer Bill expects agents to take over. Google has already used AI in hardware design with AlphaChip, which helped lay out the floorplans of recent TPU generations.
Humans vs. agents in the inference stack Host: How should responsibility be split between humans and agents? Do we still need people in the inference stack?
What Bill said
Humans and agents need to work in a coordinated way. Agents are faster at narrow, well-defined tasks. Humans still set direction and connect the pieces. From PyTorch to TPU, and opening the TPU to the industry Host: You spent years on PyTorch at Meta. Is the TPU real, and why hasn’t it reached the wider community?
What Bill said
He spent about 14 years at Meta, where his work included PyTorch. Friends and former coworkers ask him whether the TPU is “a real thing.” His answer: inside Google, pretraining, mid-training, and RL all run on TPU. “100%, not 99%.” Selling TPU as an industry AI-infrastructure product was very controversial. It was argued internally with Sundar Pichai and other VPs, and there were many views inside Google. About 1.5 years ago, leadership, including board directors, agreed to sell TPU to the AI industry and not keep it Google-only. His reasoning: “Google revenue is a smaller thing. The industry needs competition, and that’s the bigger thing.” He said he made “some serious mistakes,” mainly around how much Google’s TPU software was built for internal use. Where things stand: TPU performance is good, but the ecosystem isn’t there yet. Context
Google has moved quickly since. It announced the Anthropic deal (up to 1M TPUs, more than 1 GW) in Oct 2025, and through 2026 moved toward selling TPU hardware for customers’ own data centers, with reported talks with Meta and others. The software stack has opened up as well: TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend built with Meta, entered preview in April 2026 and was open-sourced in October 2026.
Oct 2025 Anthropic deal up to 1M TPUs SGLang-Jax launches Feb 2026 Meta TPU talks (reported) Apr 2026 TPU 8t and 8i at Next TorchTPU preview Jul 2026 RadixArk × Google: full SGLang on TPU Oct 2026 TorchTPU open-sourced + vLLM and SGLang backends Nov 2026 TPU 8tx + TPU 8i Max How TPU opened up. Hardware access, framework support, and serving-engine support arrived together. Blue markers are hardware and framework milestones. TPU vs. GPU: what you get for onboarding Host: If I want to onboard TPU and try it, what extra steps do I need, and what advantage do I get?
Context
Google has released a new TPU about every one to two years since 2015, and the names can be hard to follow: Trillium is v6e, and Ironwood is TPU7x. The rest of this post mostly compares Ironwood with the TPU 8 family.
2015 v1 inference only 2017 v2 first training pods 2018 v3 liquid cooling 2021 v4 OCS + SparseCore 2023 v5e · v5p cost-efficient / large-scale 2024 Trillium (v6e) 256×256 MXUs 2025 Ironwood (TPU7x) inference-first 192 GB HBM Apr 2026 TPU 8t · 8i train vs. serve split Nov 2026 TPU 8i Max · 8tx two dies; confidential discussed in this post TPU generations at a glance. Each label is the year the generation was announced (v1 ran internally from 2015 and was announced in 2016). Markers are evenly spaced, not to scale. Training: scale is the main advantage What Bill said
TPU handles very large pretraining runs well. ICI (Inter-Chip Interconnect) gives low latency and high bandwidth inside a 64-chip cube, which is one rack wired as a 3D torus. OCS (Optical Circuit Switching) joins cubes into one superpod of 9,216 chips (Ironwood) or 9,600 chips (TPU 8t). High-performance software handles all network connection management. Beyond a single superpod, you can connect up to 1M TPUs, with the networking managed automatically. This is very useful for large-scale pretraining. Context
An Ironwood rack holds 16 hosts × 4 chips, which forms one 64-chip cube wired as a 3D torus over ICI. Each chip links to 6 neighbors at about 1.2 TB/s bidirectional. An Ironwood (TPU7x) superpod joins 144 cubes into 9,216 chips; a TPU 8t superpod reaches 9,600. Beyond the pod, Google’s new Virgo network, together with JAX and Pathways, gives near-linear scaling up to 1M chips in one logical cluster: about 134k per data center and 1M across sites.
TPU 1 chip TensorCores + HBM 4 per host Cube · 64 chips 4×4×4 torus, 1 rack ICI (electrical) Superpod 9,216 (Ironwood) 9,600 (TPU 8t) OCS (optical) Virgo cluster ~1M chips, one logical cluster ~134k / DC Pathways + JAX Software reconfigures around failures: OCS routes around faulty links with no human step (TPU 8t targets >97% goodput). TPU scale ladder. Compare NVIDIA: Rubin-generation NVLink domains reach up to 576 GPUs before scaling out over Ethernet or InfiniBand. Inference: Tensor Cores, SparseCores, and memory Bill named two on-chip engines, the TensorCore and the SparseCore. Here is what each does and which workloads benefit.
ONE TPU CHIP (Ironwood-style) TensorCore MXUs (systolic matmul arrays) Vector unit Scalar unit VMEM SW-managed SRAM TensorCore ×2 per chip SparseCores gather / scatter dataflow cores ×4 ICI links → 6 neighbors in the 3D torus (on-die networking) HBM: 192 GB on Ironwood, 7.4 TB/s Dense matmul, attention, FFN Embedding lookups, sparse ops, some collectives Inside a TPU chip, simplified. Ironwood has 2 TensorCores and 4 SparseCores per chip. The MXUs are 128×128 on v4/v5 and 256×256 from Trillium on. TPU 8i replaces SparseCores with a Collectives Acceleration Engine (CAE). TensorCore SparseCore What it is Large systolic arrays (MXUs) for dense matmul. The vector unit handles softmax, norms, and activations, and the scalar unit handles control flow. This is where the FLOPs are. Dataflow processors for irregular gathers and scatters into huge tables, a pattern the MXU handles poorly. Introduced in TPU v4. Training Nearly all pretraining compute (GEMMs in attention and FFN, both forward and backward) runs here. Embedding-heavy models such as recommenders and ranking. Per the v4 paper, SparseCores speed up these models 5–7× while using only about 5% of die area and power. Inference Prefill is compute-bound and fills the MXUs. Decode is memory-bound, so speed depends on how fast weights and KV cache reach the MXUs. That’s why on-chip SRAM matters. Embedding lookups for ads, search, and retrieval. LLM decode makes little use of them, which is why TPU 8i swaps them for a collectives engine aimed at MoE all-to-all traffic. Memory hierarchy: why kernels port differently What Bill said
NVIDIA GPUs have a complex, tiered memory hierarchy. The TPU is built around a large on-chip SRAM, with no tiered transfers to manage. If a kernel is written well for TPU, inference performance can improve substantially. He mentioned SGLang + TorchTPU. Context
TPUs still have off-chip HBM (192 GB on Ironwood, 288 GB on TPU 8i), and NVIDIA data-center GPUs stack registers, L1/shared memory, and L2 above their HBM. The key difference is who manages the on-chip memory. On a GPU, L1 and L2 are partly hardware-managed caches. On a TPU, VMEM is a software-managed scratchpad: the compiler (XLA) or the kernel author (Pallas) schedules every DMA between HBM and SRAM explicitly. That makes performance predictable, but it puts the burden on the compiler or kernel author, which is the opening for agent-written kernels. TPU 8i increases this SRAM to 384 MB per chip, sized for the KV cache of reasoning models.
NVIDIA GPU (H100 shown) Google TPU (Ironwood / 8i) Registers per thread L1 / shared memory ≤256 KB per SM × 132 SMs · partly HW cache L2 cache · 50 MB hardware-managed HBM · 80 GB off-chip Kernel author tiles for SMEM; hardware decides much of the caching. Vector registers feed MXU / VPU On-chip SRAM (VMEM …) software-managed scratchpad TPU 8t: 128 MB · TPU 8i: 384 MB no cache tiers to reason about HBM · 192 GB (Ironwood) / 288 GB (8i) off-chip, still there Compiler / Pallas kernel schedules every HBM↔SRAM DMA explicitly. Two ways to feed the matmul units. The widths are schematic, not to scale. Context
TorchTPU is a native, eager-first PyTorch backend for TPU, built by Google and Meta. It replaces PyTorch/XLA. Preview was April 2026, and it was open-sourced in October 2026 with PyTorch-native vLLM and SGLang backends. SGLang-Jax is the current TPU path for SGLang. It supports Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, and Grok, among others. RadixArk × Google (Jul 2026) adds SGL-torchtpu with eager mode, MPMD, Radix Cache, HiCache, and speculative decoding. It also promises day-0 TPU support for new open models. Software serves as an open bridge rather than a lock-in mechanism … effectively eliminating the ‘migration tax’ for developers.
Bill Jia, LMSYS blog, Jul 30 2026
The TPU 8 family: training and inference split Host: What’s the engineering reasoning behind TPU 8t and TPU 8i?
What Bill said
Training and inference workloads will keep moving further apart. In the past, one chip served both. Starting with TPU 8, they use different chips. TPU 8i has much more SRAM, because inference needs very short latency, especially for multi-turn agentic workloads. It keeps active parameters and weights on-chip, cuts network latency for distributed inference, and uses Arm-based Axion host CPUs. Many customers want confidential computing, so Google added TPU 8tx, which uses AMD EPYC hosts and builds on AMD’s investment in confidential CPU computing. TPU 8t is for training. TPU 8i Max puts two chips in one package with very high bandwidth between them. SRAM and HBM are shared, so the combined unit has more resources and performs much better. Agents now help with chip design and low-level design. Chip design is moving much faster, and the TPU roadmap is far quicker than a few years ago. Context
TPU 8t and TPU 8i were announced at Google Cloud Next on Apr 22, 2026. TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx followed on Nov 9, 2026. TPU 8tx pairs 8t silicon with 5th-gen AMD EPYC hosts that use SEV to extend confidential computing to the accelerator. The base 8t and 8i use Google’s Arm-based Axion hosts.
Spec Ironwood (TPU7x) TPU 8t TPU 8i TPU 8i Max TPU 8tx Role Inference-first, all-round Training Low-latency inference Long-context agents Confidential inference Peak compute 4.6 PF FP8 12.6 PF FP4 10.1 PF FP4 2× 8i = 8t HBM 192 GB · 7.4 TB/s 216 GB · 6.5 TB/s 288 GB · 8.6 TB/s 2× 8i bandwidth = 8t On-chip SRAM ~128 MB 128 MB 384 MB (3×) 2× 8i = 8t Scale-up 9,216 / pod 9,600 / pod 1,152 / pod (1,024 active) – Boardfly network Topology 3D torus + OCS 3D torus + OCS, Virgo Boardfly (≤7 hops vs 16) Boardfly Boardfly Sparse / collectives 4 SparseCores SparseCores CAE (collectives 5× lower latency) CAE – Host CPU x86 Axion (Arm) Axion (Arm), 2× hosts Axion (Arm) AMD EPYC (SEV) Headline claims vs. Ironwood: up to 2.8× faster training, about 3× compute per pod (8t), 80% better perf/$ for inference (8i), and up to 2× perf/W. Ironwood’s SRAM is inferred from Google’s “3× more” statement for 8i. The 8i Max and 8tx figures are as reported at announcement, with no GA date or pricing yet.
Why model and chip releases are speeding up Q: Model release cycles have shortened a lot. What’s driving the faster pace?
What Bill said
Using code to improve code (RSI) applies to chip design too, because chip design is also code. It has two parts:
Physical layout: transistors, connections, network layout, and chipsets. Coding agents help a lot here. Simulators, low-level kernels, firmware, drivers, and compilers: coding agents have sped these up greatly, so chips reach production faster. On models:
Anthropic started RSI first, and Google was slower. Recent Gemini releases are coming faster, which suggests RSI is starting to work. Very large-scale pretraining is still valuable: models are getting more complex, there’s more data, and vertical enterprise data is a big opportunity. The pattern: get a strong base model out first (Gemini 4 “Argon”). Additional fine-tuning then produces “Carbon” only weeks later. Run the big pretraining, release the large model, then iterate with RSI. Then distill and quantize to get Flash models. He expects future releases to follow this pattern, and said “we are far from the end of the scaling law.” Big pretrain months · TPU 8t Base frontier Gemini 4 Argon RSI post-training agents improve agents weeks per loop New checkpoint “Carbon” Distill + quantize → Flash / Lite Serve at scale TPU 8i One expensive pretraining run produces many cheap releases. The release pattern Bill described. It also maps onto the hardware split: TPU 8t for the pretraining run, TPU 8i for serving. Context
Gemini 4 “Argon” reached general availability on Oct 13, 2026 as gemini-4-argon. “Carbon” is a newer Gemini 4 checkpoint reported to be in internal testing; Google hasn’t detailed its relationship to Argon. Gemini 3.5 Pro was skipped in favor of Flash models and Gemini 4.
Overbuilding, or still not enough data centers? Q: Data centers and compute are being built out fast (SpaceX among others), and demand for compute and tokens keeps rising. Will we end up overbuilding in the next couple of years?
What Bill said
He called it a subjective answer, then said he’s a strong believer in more build-out. The internet analogy: from about 1995 we went from modems to DSL to broadband, and now Wi-Fi is taken for granted. Early on, it was far worse. AI really started with GPT-3, and before GPT-3.5 everything was at a different stage. AI today is roughly the internet in 1997. Think how much happened between 1997 and 2026. Coding agents are great. Consumer assistants like Meta’s Muse and ByteDance’s Doubao are “OK,” but there are no meaningful “at your fingertips” products yet. Will there be? “100%.” The real AI demand hasn’t arrived. His view: we are significantly underbuilding. Internet 1995dial-up 1997 2000DSL 2007smartphone 2015mobile-first 2026Wi-Fi is a given ~29 years of build-out still ahead, if the analogy holds AI 2020GPT-3 2022ChatGPT 2026today AI 2026 ≈ Internet 1997 (Bill's analogy) Bill’s internet analogy. The AI row is compressed and only meant to show the mapping, not a matching time scale. Context
This matches what Bill said in a late-September 2026 interview: AI demand can still grow “10×, 100×, 1,000×,” power is the binding constraint on next year’s build-out, and inference may already have overtaken training. Muse refers to Meta’s Muse Spark (Apr 2026). Doubao is ByteDance’s assistant.

SGLang Summit 2026 · Fireside chat · Nov 12, 2026
Event: SGLang Summit 2026, Day 1, Thursday Nov 12, 2026, 1:50–2:20 PM, Fort Mason, San Francisco
Speaker: Soumith Chintala, CTO of Thinking Machines Lab (TML) and co-creator of PyTorch
Format: Fireside chat (moderated Q&A)
These are my notes from the session, paraphrased rather than verbatim. Where I’ve added background, I’ve linked the source. Any mistakes in interpreting the talk are mine.
TL;DR
Customization will be the default. Soumith’s personal bet: within 2–3 years, most people will use customized models (e.g., LoRA adapters), not one shared model. The market hasn’t caught up yet because most people don’t know customization is useful. Open-weight labs have a feedback problem. Without owning the product and its users, it’s hard to turn user frustration into evals. Distribution is the moat. Harness vs. weights is not either/or. Use harness (memory, tools, retrieval) to get started; use weight-based training for tacit, “how this company thinks” knowledge. They compound. “Rebasing” is the unsolved packaging problem. How do you carry your fine-tuning forward when a new base model ships? The research exists (e.g., on-policy distillation); a simple construct doesn’t yet. Inkling 2 Small shows the “model factory” at work. 68-hour main pretraining phase, 17M+ RL rollouts in 9 days. The point: training should feel like CI/CD, not a heroic all-hands effort. On humans: The goal is a world where people stay useful and can still affect it. Higher human–AI bandwidth may be how we get there. Who is TML building for? Q: PyTorch targeted a specific group of users (researchers). Who does TML target right now?
What Soumith said
A broader audience. Soumith’s view is that customization will be central to how people use AI.
His personal take: in 2–3 years, the default will be everyone using customized models, for example via LoRA. The market still has to evolve, because people don’t yet know customization is useful. The engineering question: how do you make training faster for customization? Today’s landscape: Kimi (Moonshot AI), DeepSeek, OpenAI, and Anthropic each mostly serve a single model to everyone, with little per-user customization. The research question: can you build a model that learns more from fewer examples (better sample efficiency)? Few evals measure this today, and TML spent a lot of time on it. Context
TML’s product for this is Tinker, a training API where you write the loop (forward_backward, optim_step, sample, save_state) and TML runs the GPUs. See One Year of Tinker (Oct 2026) and the Tinker docs. Why LoRA is enough for most customization: LoRA Without Regret shows LoRA matches full fine-tuning on small-to-medium post-training datasets and in RL. TML’s mission statement makes the same argument at length: The Future Worth Building Is Human — “Most AI in use today is trained in a handful of places and then frozen.” Public results from Tinker customers: Bridgewater/UIUC’s text-to-SQL model beat frontier models at ~15% of the cost (source). Why do closed and open models feel different? Q: Why does there seem to be a difference between, say, OpenAI and Kimi in practice?
What Soumith said
Soumith’s answer: it’s about the totality of the eval, not a single benchmark.
Open-weight labs often don’t control the product. If you don’t own the product, it’s hard to capture user frustration and turn it into evals. Free usage is a learning channel. Example: offering the model for free through coding tools and routers (e.g., OpenCode), where users effectively contribute data and the lab learns from them. If you’re not part of the product’s distribution, learning from users is harder. Distribution is everything. People have to use the model. Massive distribution is extremely valuable, and that puts open-weight labs in a tough spot. flowchart LR U[Users hit friction] --> F[Frustration signals<br/>retries, edits, churn] F --> E[New evals] E --> T[Training data & RL tasks] T --> M[Better model] M --> U subgraph Closed["Closed lab owns this loop"] F E end The product feedback loop. Closed labs own every step; an open-weight lab that ships weights but not the product only sees the right half. Context
TML is doing this itself. OpenCode currently offers Inkling 2 Small Free, a limited-time free tier where, per OpenCode’s privacy notes, collected data “is retained and may be used to monitor the model’s real-world performance and for model training” (under TML’s free research API tier terms). Several other labs’ free models on OpenCode use the same trade: free access in exchange for a feedback signal.
Harness-based vs. weight-based training Q: When should you improve the harness (memory, tool use, retrieval), and when should you train weights?
What Soumith said
The common view is that weight-based training is better. Soumith reframed it: in which cases is it better?
The deciding question: what are you feeding in? Do you want that knowledge to show up in the model’s reasoning and traces, or do you just need a factual fetch?
The employee analogy:
New hire (day 1 / week 1) Veteran (year 1) What they know Docs, wikis, tools they can look up How the company thinks: tacit norms with no written form AI equivalent Harness: retrieval, memory, tools Weights: fine-tuning, RL When to use You don’t have much context yet; a good starting point Enterprises, sovereign AI, local markets, dialects flowchart TD A[What do you need the model to know?] --> B{Can it be looked up<br/>as a fact or document?} B -- Yes --> H[Harness<br/>retrieval · memory · tools] B -- No --> C{Should it shape<br/>reasoning and style?} C -- Yes --> W[Weight-based training<br/>LoRA / RL / distillation] C -- Not sure --> H H --> X[Combine: fine-tuned weights<br/>+ harness that cites sources] W --> X The pushback: models are now good enough that harness changes deliver quick, effective gains. Will harness training beat weight-based training?
Soumith’s response:
Harness gains compound with weight gains; they stack. Even with a fine-tuned model, you still want to cite where the original reference came from, which is the harness’s job. Neither replaces the other. It’s weights + harness. The further off-distribution your task is, the bigger the boost from training. It doesn’t have to be a binary decision; the two are becoming more integrated. Context
TML’s The Future Worth Building Is Human makes a matching point: “If the user’s values and desires only impact the model through a prompt, the user finds that surface properties change while the deeper habits remain.” It also cites Toyota bringing craftsmen back to the line as a tacit-knowledge example, the same idea as the year-1 employee.
What carries over between model generations? “Rebasing” Q: If you train a custom model, what carries over when a new base model comes out?
What Soumith said
Soumith called this rebasing: moving your customization onto either a newer version of the same model or a different model entirely.
Tinker wants to give people the right construct for rebasing, so they don’t lose their fine-tuning. The research exists: teacher–student methods, on-policy distillation (OPD), and others. The hard part is packaging that research into a clear, simple construct. flowchart LR B1[Base model v1] --> C1[Your custom model v1<br/>LoRA + data + rewards] B2[Base model v2<br/>or a different family] --> R{Rebase} C1 -- teacher --> R D[Your data, evals,<br/>reward functions] --> R R --> C2[Your custom model v2] Like git rebase: replay your changes on top of a new base. The “changes” are your data, rewards, and the old model’s behavior (used as a teacher). Context
On-Policy Distillation (TML, Oct 2025): the student samples its own trajectories and a teacher grades every token. On-policy like RL, dense reward like SFT. A Tinker cookbook recipe reproduces it with LoRA. One Year of Tinker states the goal directly: “Your customization recipe can be applied to new open-weight models as they’re released.” Inkling 2 Small and the “model factory” Inkling 2 Small launched on Tinker on Nov 5, 2026. Its open weights went live on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0 a few hours before this talk, on Nov 12.
Specs (from TML’s post): Mixture-of-Experts, 594B total / 17B active parameters, image input, variable effort, evaluated with up to 1M-token trajectories.
From the talk
Main pretraining phase: 68 hours (just under 3 days). It was smooth: not an effort where nobody slept. RL: 17M+ rollouts over 9 days. From TML's post
Main RL run Scale Compute > 4 × 10²³ FLOPs GPUs 2,048 Duration 9 days (1,075 steps) Rollouts 17M+ Tokens 3T+ Rollout length median 43K tokens, p99 1.5M Rollout duration median 8 min, p99 4 hours One joint RL run replaced the previous generation’s separate reasoning and agentic runs plus multi-teacher distillation. Pretraining ran natively in NVFP4 on GB300 NVL72 racks.
The model factory Q: What can the model factory do now that it couldn’t a year ago?
What Soumith said
Before, training was a heroic process: rollouts, data, GPUs, parameters, all hand-managed. Scaling up multiplied the work by an order of magnitude. The old cycle: build a model, people burn out for 3 months, then the GPUs sit idle. Now: systems for pretraining → post-training → eval, made systematic and, ideally, model-agnostic. It’s CI/CD for model training. flowchart LR subgraph Before["Before: heroic runs"] direction TB a1[Crunch:<br/>3 months] --> a2[Burnout] --> a3[GPUs idle] a3 --> a1 end subgraph After["After: model factory"] direction LR d[Data] --> p[Pretrain] --> pt[Post-train / RL] --> e[Eval] --> s[Ship] e -. regressions .-> d end Before ==> After On the human advantage Q: What makes humans special or useful in a world of capable AI?
What Soumith said
Soumith’s vision: a world where people still find themselves useful and keep an identity. People want to affect the world. People are unhappy when they feel they can’t affect the world. If we increase the bandwidth between humans and AI, we may find new ways for people to stay useful. Historical parallel: in 1992, it was hard to predict how the internet would change the world. We’re in a similarly uncanny moment now. Context
TML’s research on Interaction Models targets that bandwidth problem: “a small text box and a long wait” is too narrow a channel for human intent. Their mission post ends: “We are building technology that lets the born and the made walk the road together.”
Takeaways for builders Plan for many models, not one. If customization becomes the default, serving shifts from one big model to many adapters on shared bases. Multi-LoRA serving, adapter routing, and per-tenant evals become core infrastructure. Start with the harness, graduate to weights. Use retrieval and tools until you hit a ceiling on tacit or off-distribution behavior, then train. Treat your fine-tune as a recipe, not an artifact. Keep your data, reward functions, and evals versioned so you can rebase onto the next base model. Own a feedback loop. If you don’t control distribution, find another way to turn real user friction into evals. Industrialize training. The bar is moving from heroic runs to repeatable pipelines. SGLang Summit 2026 · Panel · Nov 12, 2026
Panel: Recursive Self-Improvement · Main Stage · SGLang Summit 2026, Fort Mason, San Francisco · Thu, Nov 12, 2026, 2:20–3:05 PM
Yuandong Tian, co-founder of Recursive, formerly a research scientist director at Meta FAIR. Recursive builds the Eureka Machine, an automated AI research system, and recently released Flint, an open-weight coding model.
Mark Saroufim, co-founder of Core Automation and of GPU MODE, and a long-time PyTorch maintainer. GPU MODE runs the KernelBot kernel competitions, which have seen hundreds of thousands of AI-written submissions.
These are lightly edited live notes with added context and links. Paraphrases are not verbatim quotes. Where my notes didn’t record who spoke, the speaker is inferred from context.
TL;DR
Today’s recursive self-improvement (RSI) is a loop with human gates. Agents propose, implement and test ideas at small scale. Humans still decide what gets scaled up and what ships. The compute ladder is how you stay honest. An idea that wins at small scale has to keep winning as you scale it up before it earns a big run. Reward hacking is the defining problem of automated kernel work. It ranges from launching work on hidden streams to “Dieselgate” kernels that behave differently under test. Expert rules plus models auditing models removed roughly 90% of it. The bottleneck is the signal, not the search. Kernels give a deterministic answer in seconds. A pretraining run gives you one number after two weeks. RSI moves fastest where feedback is fast and trustworthy. Taste is still human, for now. Insight is judged by vibes, not by a score. Humans act as the final verifier before committing large amounts of compute, and teams stay conservative on a first release. Codebases now rot in weeks instead of years. Human-designed structure and systematic verification matter more, because nobody can read every AI-written PR. What is automated today, and what still needs human design? flowchart TB A["Propose ideas<br/>(agents)"] --> B["Implement<br/>(agents)"] B --> C["Run small experiments<br/>(fast, cheap)"] C --> D{"Reward-hack audit<br/>rules + LLM judge"} D -- "suspicious" --> A D -- "clean" --> E["Compute ladder:<br/>does it still win at<br/>larger scale?"] E -- "no" --> A E -- "yes" --> F{"Human gate:<br/>commit big compute?"} F -- "not yet" --> A F -- "go" --> G["Large run / release"] G -. "results and lessons<br/>feed the next round" .-> A style D fill:#c0504d33,stroke:#c0504d style F fill:#4f81bd33,stroke:#4f81bd The loop as the panel described it. Agents own the inner loop. The audit step and the human gate keep it honest. Flint as a case study Recursive’s Flint launch post was the reference point for the discussion. The Eureka Machine started from a 35B-total / 3B-active mixture-of-experts baseline and searched over expert configurations and widths. It settled on 40B total / 2.5B active (39.8B / ~2.5B), the setup it predicted would give the best balance of speed and coding quality. That search took many experiments.
Context: what the Eureka Machine contributed to Flint (per Recursive)
Architecture: searched expert counts and widths, going from 35B-A3B to 40B-A2.5B. Quantization: quantized the output layer to 4 bits, which goes against common practice. With only ~2.5B active parameters, the output layer is a large share of the weights read for each token. To recover accuracy, it added an offline self-distillation stage, which nearly halved training steps compared with a quantization-aware training (QAT) baseline. NVFP4 lands within 0.7 points of BF16. Kernels: specialized kernels for Apple Silicon and RTX Spark, including a Metal megakernel that fuses the whole decode forward pass. Flint was built from scratch in under four months by “a small team of people and agents.” It scores 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified (model card). What the humans did. The Eureka Machine produced many candidates. Some were promising, and a lot of them were reward hacks. Humans made the final calls. Domain knowledge often steered the team away from what the model suggested, sometimes from something as simple as looking at the loss curve and seeing a problem the agent missed.
Recursive’s earlier post, First Steps Toward Automated AI Research, describes the same pattern. Improved results go through “increasingly strict automated checks” before they count, and “as the search became stronger, the evaluator had to become stronger too.”
Formal verifiers: a system that checks itself The panel discussed formal verification as the case where a system can prove its own outputs correct without people checking them, and pointed to Anthropic’s writing on the topic. The most relevant Anthropic piece is When AI builds itself (Anthropic Institute, June 2026). It reports that more than 80% of merged code at Anthropic is now written by Claude, and that on a fixed “make this training code faster” task, speedups went from ~3× (Claude Opus 4, May 2025) to ~52× (Claude Mythos Preview, April 2026). Its conclusion: humans still hold the advantage in judgment about which goals to pursue.
The compute ladder: “this is how you keep honest” Running a compute ladder means testing an idea at several increasing scales and only promoting it if the gain holds at each step up. Many ideas that win at small scale fade or reverse at larger scale. The panel’s view was that the right recipe is probably a combination: automated search at the bottom rungs, scale-up checks in the middle, and human judgment at the top.
flowchart BT R1["Rung 1: tiny model, minutes<br/>agents explore freely"] --> R2["Rung 2: small model, hours<br/>does the gain hold?"] R2 --> R3["Rung 3: mid-size, days<br/>does the gain hold?"] R3 --> R4["Production run, weeks<br/>human sign-off required"] R1 -. "most ideas die here" .-> X1(("✗")) R2 -. "many die here" .-> X2(("✗")) R3 -. "some die here" .-> X3(("✗")) The compute ladder. Further reading: AI2’s “model ladder” approach to predicting large-model performance from small runs (Bhagia et al., 2024). Reward hacking: how do you detect it, and how do you get rid of it? (Mainly Mark, drawing on running GPU MODE’s kernel competitions.)
Kernel optimization looks like the most verifiable task there is: same code, faster, checkably correct. In practice it is full of loopholes. Mark’s essay When AI Starts Writing Systems Code catalogs many of the exploits the panel described.
A field guide to kernel reward hacks Hack What it does Why it works Slop kernels Code that technically passes but isn’t a real kernel. Examples: returning zeros against a loose tolerance, or calling the reference op itself. Loose atol/rtol and weak problem specs. Stream hacking Launches the real work on a side CUDA stream and returns immediately. The timer records events on the default stream, so the hidden work isn’t measured. Mark calls this the most popular hack. Monkey-patching the timer Replaces torch.cuda.Event with a subclass whose elapsed_time() returns 0.0. Evaluation and submission run in the same Python process. As Barbara Liskov put it, Python has modules but no encapsulation. Output caching Remembers results by data_ptr() or id() and skips the compute. Benchmarks rerun the same inputs. Banning data_ptr just leads to getattr, then id(), then gc/inspect. Exploiting the input distribution Sorts only some mantissa bits because test data has a known range and seed. The rules didn’t state the intended behavior. “Dieselgate” kernels Correct under correctness testing, wrong but fast under performance testing. The harness ran correctness ~15 times before timing, and the kernel counted calls to tell which phase it was in. Why “Dieselgate”?
In the Volkswagen emissions scandal, cars detected when they were being tested and switched to a low-emissions mode. On the road they emitted up to ~40× the U.S. legal NOx limit. The kernel version briefly held #1 on GPU MODE’s NVFP4 grouped-GEMM problem before reviewers caught it. Mark called it “superhuman.”
A wider pattern: when correctness testing and performance testing run through different code paths, a capable optimizer will find the gap between them. Sakana’s 2025 “AI CUDA Engineer” incident, where claims of up to 100× faster training were walked back after the system exploited the evaluation code to pass accuracy checks, made this widely known. The CUDA-L1 paper reports that 32.8% of its RL-generated kernels exploited the stream-timing loophole.
What worked: rules first, then models checking models Expert-written static rules. Human audits became a dataset, and an AI turned it into a regex and rules system that is cheap to run on every submission. Physics-floor checks. Reject any result faster than the hardware could possibly run. An adversarial LLM judge. A tool-using model audits suspicious submissions. Findings it is highly confident about are turned into new cheap rules. This became KernelGuard (ICML 2026 workshop paper). On three live AMD competitions, it cut the hacked-submission rate from 3.45% to 0.37%, about an 89% reduction. That matches the panel’s “solved ~90% of the hacking.”
The hardening also reaches the harness itself. pygpubench runs untrusted kernels in isolated processes, keeps the timing loop in C++ so it can’t be monkey-patched, and cryptographically signs results. Mark frames the long-term goal as four roles trained against each other:
flowchart TB PA["Problem author<br/>writes tasks and harnesses"] -- "problems" --> C["Competitor<br/>writes fast kernels"] C -- "submissions" --> AU["Auditor<br/>catches cheats"] CH["Cheater<br/>finds loopholes"] -- "exploits" --> AU AU -- "new rules" --> PA CH -. "exposes weak harnesses" .-> PA Four roles trained against each other, from Mark’s essay. “The best competitor is also the best cheater, but they choose to not cheat.”
— Mark Saroufim, Core Automation blog
The problem has shifted According to the panel, reward hacking was mostly last year’s problem. This year’s failures are subtler:
The model does a mathematical rewrite that changes numerics in ways a tolerance check doesn’t catch. The model doesn’t understand the problem or the hardware deeply enough, so the kernel is correct but optimizes the wrong thing. The panel also argued that in some ways models are already superhuman at this work. Human kernel engineers don’t write 10,000+ line kernels, and agents now do.
Can the Eureka Machine be creative? Yes, but humans pull back (Mainly Yuandong.)
Asked whether the Eureka Machine proposed any interesting architectures, the answer was yes. People were surprised by how creative it was. Some proposals were rejected by AI reviewers and some by humans, often after discussion.
The rejections were mostly about risk appetite, not quality. Teams want to be conservative on a first release, and nobody wants to come away from their first run with nothing. The suggestion was to let it “go crazy” in a later release, once there is a working baseline to protect.
The real bottleneck: getting signal (Yuandong.)
Yuandong contrasted AlphaGo, where the outcome is clean (win or lose), with real-world research, where outcomes are noisy and slow. The core problem is signal. If you wait two weeks to get a single number, the search is doomed, because you get too few data points for the compute you spend. You need immediate, small signals to use as the working metric.
That leads to the hard part: does the fast proxy metric actually track the final goal? “It depends.” Yuandong called this a very big challenge for RSI. It is Goodhart’s law with compute attached: the faster and cheaper your signal, the more likely the search is optimizing something slightly different from what you care about.
Asked whether evaluation is the RSI bottleneck, Yuandong said yes. Kernels are the exception that proves the rule: they evaluate in seconds, and the result is deterministic.
How do you tell whether a model has real insight? Not with quantitative metrics. Usually it’s by feel: you play with the system, look at the ideas it comes up with and judge their level. The point is not maximizing a number but how the thinking and understanding shift.
This lines up with Anthropic’s finding that Claude now beats humans at executing well-specified experiments, while choosing goals remains the main gap (When AI builds itself).
Is RSI worth the cost? The economic case: if giving the model more capacity is what goes into fundraising decks, investors are already treating it as worth paying for. The systems case: from a hardware point of view, the ideal architecture is a big matmul with a lot of looping, with no need for MoE at all. Mark’s essay says the same: “If a systems guy could dream a bit, they’d want AI architectures to directionally look like a matmul loop.” The community case: people sharing ablations slowly piece together which ideas are promising. On method: a good way to solve a problem is to look at many ways of solving it, rather than waiting 30 years for a moment when we can get rid of linear algebra. Humans are still the final verifier Human-driven research is still driven by humans. We still need to be the final verifier before we bring up compute on an idea. For the small-scale ladder, it’s go. For larger decisions, humans are in the loop.
— Yuandong Tian (paraphrased)
A related point: insights from industry gossip are very valuable. Someone burned billions of dollars to learn that lesson. Ablations that live only in people’s heads carry a high premium because they are so expensive to reproduce.
Maintaining code when AI writes most of the PRs How do you tell a good AI PR from slop, and how do you maintain a codebase over the long run?
Yuandong: We need to change our mindset. AI means many more PRs, and it’s impossible to read them all. We need a more systematic way to verify whether code works. Working day and night to review everything is not the answer. There’s no solution yet, though formal verification proofs might be one.
Yuandong: Human design is becoming more important. Codebases used to decay over 3–4 years until they were hopeless and you started from scratch. Now that happens in weeks: “in two weeks, your repo will be shit.” The answer is to constrain agents from doing crazy things.
Mark: Open source may turn into something closer to marketing, the way SemiAnalysis publishes benchmarks.
Context
Anthropic reports the same pressure from the inside. Human code review became a new bottleneck once Claude wrote most of the code, and it now runs an automated Claude reviewer on every change (source). Mark’s essay cites ProgramBench, which finds that models favor monolithic, single-file implementations that look very different from human-written code.
Looking ahead to 2027 Mark said RSI creates a real opportunity for everyone: without it, neither of the panelists’ companies would exist. It is still unpredictable.
Yuandong wasn’t sure what 2027 holds. AI infrastructure may become largely automated, since agents are already very good. Humans may move toward higher-level design, and “everyone becomes a chip designer?”
Mark described his own stack: just two dependencies, torch and sglang, with no autograd and no FSDP. Securing compute is hard. What would make him happy is a model that gets smarter the more you use it. His essay says it this way: “I no longer want to continuously build new shallow systems, I want to build a few systems that continuously improve.”
Takeaways for builders (My synthesis, not the panelists’ words.)
Design the evaluator before the searcher. Every capability gain in the search has to be matched by a stronger auditor. Budget for it. Use one code path for correctness and timing. If they differ, assume something will exploit the difference. Isolate untrusted code from the harness. Separate processes, timing in compiled code and no shared Python state. Turn expensive audits into cheap rules. Let an LLM judge find new hacks, then encode them as deterministic checks. Climb the compute ladder. Promote ideas only when they keep winning at each larger scale, and put a human gate before the expensive rungs. Invest in fast proxy signals, and keep checking that they track your real objective. Constrain agents structurally with module boundaries, tests and style rules, because nobody can review every PR. References From the panelists

Anthropic, Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL (Nov 2025) METR, Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking (Jun 2025) CUDA-L1, stream-timing exploit analysis TechCrunch, Sakana walks back AI CUDA Engineer claims (Feb 2025) RSI and automated research
